--- title: "Creating Data Frames in R" date: "1/6/2025" date-modified: last-modified date-format: long --- # Creating Data Frames in R ## Introduction ### Overview Creating data frames is fundamental in R for managing and analyzing tabular data. This tutorial explores: - **Base R Functions:** `data.frame()` and `as.data.frame()`. - **`tidyverse` Functions:** `tibble::tibble()` and `dplyr::data_frame()`. Data frames allow structured data storage, enabling row and column manipulations akin to spreadsheets. ### Use Cases - Cleaning and structuring raw data. - Aggregating results from computations. - Preparing data for visualization or modeling. ### Benefits - **Base R:** Straightforward and widely supported. - **`tidyverse`:** Intuitive syntax, compatibility with the pipe operator `|>`, and enhanced features like printing. ## Getting Started ### Loading the Package ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Use pacman to load packages pacman::p_load(tidyverse) ``` ::: ### Basic Usage in Base R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create a simple data frame data_base <- data.frame( Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"), Age = c(25, 30, 35), Score = c(85.5, 90.3, 78.9) ) data_base ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Name | Age| Score| |:-------|---:|-----:| |Alice | 25| 85.5| |Bob | 30| 90.3| |Charlie | 35| 78.9|
::: ::: ### Basic Usage in `tidyverse` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create a tibble data_tidy <- tibble::tibble( Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"), Age = c(25, 30, 35), Score = c(85.5, 90.3, 78.9) ) data_tidy ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Name | Age| Score| |:-------|---:|-----:| |Alice | 25| 85.5| |Bob | 30| 90.3| |Charlie | 35| 78.9|
::: ::: ## Key Functions and Features ### Base R Functions #### Description `data.frame()` creates data frames from vectors or lists. #### Syntax ```r #| echo: fenced data.frame(x, ..., row.names = NULL, check.rows = FALSE, check.names = TRUE) ``` #### Example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data_example <- data.frame( ID = 1:3, Category = c("A", "B", "A"), Value = c(100, 200, 150) ) data_example ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| ID|Category | Value| |--:|:--------|-----:| | 1|A | 100| | 2|B | 200| | 3|A | 150|
::: ::: ### `tidyverse` Functions #### Description `tibble::tibble()` constructs modern data frames with automatic column type detection. #### Syntax ```r tibble::tibble(...) ``` #### Example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data_tidy_example <- tibble::tibble( ID = 1:3, Category = c("A", "B", "A"), Value = c(100, 200, 150) ) data_tidy_example ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| ID|Category | Value| |--:|:--------|-----:| | 1|A | 100| | 2|B | 200| | 3|A | 150|
::: ::: ## In-Depth Examples ### Example 1: Joining Data Frames #### Objective Combine two data frames by a common key. #### Steps ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df1 <- tibble::tibble(ID = 1:3, Value1 = c(10, 20, 30)) df2 <- tibble::tibble(ID = 2:4, Value2 = c(40, 50, 60)) merged <- dplyr::left_join(df1, df2, by = "ID") merged ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| ID| Value1| Value2| |--:|------:|------:| | 1| 10| NA| | 2| 20| 40| | 3| 30| 50|
::: ::: #### Output Observe how `NA` fills for unmatched rows. ### Example 2: Filtering and Selecting #### Objective Filter rows where `Value1 > 15` and select specific columns. #### Steps ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} filtered <- merged |> dplyr::filter(Value1 > 15) |> dplyr::select(ID, Value1) filtered ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| ID| Value1| |--:|------:| | 2| 20| | 3| 30|
::: ::: ## Advanced Features ### Customization #### Adjust Column Names ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} colnames(data_base) <- c("FullName", "Years", "ExamScore") data_base ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|FullName | Years| ExamScore| |:--------|-----:|---------:| |Alice | 25| 85.5| |Bob | 30| 90.3| |Charlie | 35| 78.9|
::: ::: #### Add Calculated Columns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data_tidy <- data_tidy |> dplyr::mutate(Grade = ifelse(Score > 80, "Pass", "Fail")) data_tidy ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Name | Age| Score|Grade | |:-------|---:|-----:|:-----| |Alice | 25| 85.5|Pass | |Bob | 30| 90.3|Pass | |Charlie | 35| 78.9|Fail |
::: ::: ### Integration with Visualization Generate a plot from the data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(data_tidy, ggplot2::aes(x = Age, y = Score)) + ggplot2::geom_point() + ggplot2::labs(title = "Age vs. Score", x = "Age", y = "Score") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](r-data-frames-basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Optimization Tips - Use `data.table` for large data sets. - Predefine column types for better memory usage. ## Troubleshooting and FAQs ### Common Issues 1. **Data Mismatch:** Ensure column lengths match when creating data frames. ```r # Error example # data.frame(a = 1:3, b = 1:4) ``` 2. **Type Conversion Warnings:** Avoid unintended type coercion by specifying `stringsAsFactors = FALSE`. ### FAQs - **Why use `tibble`?** `tibble` provides cleaner, more readable output, and better handling of column names and types. ## Best Practices - Use consistent column names and data types. - Validate data integrity before further processing. - Leverage `tidyverse` pipes for readability and maintainability. ## Conclusion ### Summary - Base R is great for quick setups and legacy code. - `tidyverse` excels for scalable, readable, and modern workflows. ### Next Steps Explore advanced techniques like `data.table` or `R6` for complex data operations. ## References and Resources - [Base R Documentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/) - [Tidyverse Guide](https://www.tidyverse.org/) - [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/)
